repo.name: TaskPilot
repo.description: Personal productivity web app (.NET 10 / ASP.NET Core Razor Pages) for managing tasks via web UI and a REST/MCP API for LLM clients.

areas.TASKS: Task CRUD, lifecycle, completion, cloning, recurrence, filtering/sorting, and the task list/board views.
areas.TAGS: User-owned tags (create/list/update/delete), per-user name uniqueness, and tag-to-task assignment.
areas.TASKTYPES: The read-only standard task-type lookup (Task/Goal/Habit/Meeting/Note/Event) and active/sort rules.
areas.AUTH: Registration, login/logout, password change, and the authenticated "me" account endpoint.
areas.APIKEYS: API key generation, listing, rename, activate/deactivate, and revoke for REST/MCP access.
areas.AUDIT: The LLM audit dashboard and the audit-log read/summary API (API access history).
areas.ACTIVITYLOG: Per-task change history (field-level old/new value log) and its read API.
areas.DASHBOARD: The home dashboard — summary cards, charts, quick-add, and deep links into filtered task views.
areas.SETTINGS: Settings page — API key management, appearance, password change, and tag management.
areas.INTEGRATIONS: The integrations/docs page (API quick-start, client snippets, MCP client config).
areas.CHANGELOG: The user-facing changelog page and the SemVer-ordered release-notes service.
areas.HEALTH: Health/diagnostics endpoints (live/ready/full/version/assets), checks, and the public health page.
areas.STATS: Statistics aggregation feeding the dashboard charts (counts, breakdowns, time series).
areas.MCP: The Model Context Protocol server tools exposing task operations to LLM clients.
areas.LAYOUT: Responsive layout and task-page view-state behavior (scope/board columns, filter persistence).
areas.SEC: Cross-cutting security invariants (authentication, authorization, owner-scoping, API-key hashing).
areas.API: Cross-cutting API-contract invariants (response envelope, error shape, pagination metadata).
areas.DATA: Cross-cutting data-integrity invariants (soft-delete, audit-write, timestamp/LastModifiedBy stamping).

requirements.statement: The total page count for a paged activity-log result is the ceiling of total record count divided by page size, clamped to a minimum of 1 (an empty result reports 1 total page).
requirements.why: SUGGESTED: Clamping the page count to a minimum of 1 keeps the pager well-formed even when a user has no activity.

requirements.statement: On key generation the service persists only an HMAC-SHA256 hash of the plain-text key (a 64-character lowercase hex string) — never the plain-text key — and the stored hash equals HMAC-SHA256 of the plain-text key under the configured secret.
requirements.why: Storing only a keyed hash means a database leak cannot expose usable credentials, per the never-store-plaintext rule.

requirements.statement: Key validation succeeds only for an active key whose HMAC-SHA256 hash matches a stored key, returning that key's name, owning user id, and key id; an inactive key or an unknown (no hash match) key validates as invalid with null name, user id, and key id.
requirements.why: This is the authentication gate for the REST API — only an active, hash-matching key may act on its owner's behalf, and inactive or unknown keys must be rejected.

requirements.statement: A newly generated plain-text key is derived from 32 cryptographically random bytes encoded as URL-safe Base64 (standard Base64 with '+' replaced by '-', '/' replaced by '_', and all '=' padding removed); the stored keyPrefix is the first 8 characters of this plain-text key.
requirements.why: 32 bytes of CSPRNG entropy makes keys infeasible to guess, and a URL-safe encoding lets the key be passed in headers without escaping.

requirements.statement: A newly created API key is active (IsActive = true) by default; deactivating a key sets IsActive = false and reactivating sets it back to true, and only active keys validate successfully (an explicitly deactivated key is treated as invalid).
requirements.why: Active-by-default makes a freshly created key immediately usable, while the active/inactive flag gives owners a reversible kill switch enforced at validation.

requirements.statement: The total page count for a paged audit-log result is the ceiling of total record count divided by page size (e.g. 5 records at page size 3 yields 2 pages).
requirements.why: SUGGESTED: A correct page count lets the audit-log pager show the right number of pages so the owner can reach every record.

requirements.statement: In the audit usage summary, totalRequests counts all of the user's API access logs across all time, whereas getsToday and writesToday count only logs whose Timestamp falls on or after the current UTC calendar date (DateTime.UtcNow.Date); getsToday counts requests with HttpMethod equal to "GET" and writesToday counts requests with any other HttpMethod, and activeApiKeys counts the user's keys whose IsActive is true.
requirements.why: SUGGESTED: These definitions back the dashboard summary cards — separating all-time totals from today's reads vs writes and counting only live keys gives the owner a meaningful activity snapshot.

requirements.statement: A paged audit-log result whose total record count is zero reports a total page count of 1 (the ceiling computation is bypassed and clamped to 1 for the empty case).
requirements.why: SUGGESTED: Clamping the empty case to one page keeps the pager well-formed (never zero pages) when there is no activity.

requirements.statement: The changelog service parses the release-notes JSON into version entries (each with version, release date, version type, summary, and a list of changes each having a type and description); valid JSON yields the versions, and empty or malformed JSON yields an empty list without throwing.
requirements.why: Tolerating empty or malformed release-notes JSON keeps the changelog page from crashing on a hand-edited or partially-deployed file.

requirements.statement: The changelog service orders versions in descending SemVer order by parsing each version into numeric (major, minor, patch) components rather than ordinal-string comparison, so "1.10" sorts above "1.9" above "1.8" and "1.10.10" above "1.10.1" above "1.10.0"; a version that cannot be parsed falls back to zero components and sorts after all well-formed entries.
requirements.why: Ordinal-string sorting would place v1.9 above v1.10; numeric SemVer ordering ensures the newest release shows first.

requirements.statement: The changelog service's "get latest" returns the highest-SemVer version entry (not the lexicographically largest), and returns null when there are no versions.
requirements.why: "Latest version" surfaces (e.g. the sidebar/what's-new hint) must reflect the true newest release, not the lexicographically largest string.

requirements.statement: A version entry exposes an "is major" flag that is true only when its version type is "major" and false for other version types (e.g. "minor").
requirements.why: SUGGESTED: The is-major flag drives the "Major" badge so major releases are visually distinguished from minor/patch ones.

requirements.statement: BuildInfo reads build metadata from the assembly: Version is a non-empty SemVer-shaped string (Major.Minor.Patch); GitCommit is either a 40-char lowercase hex SHA or "unknown"; GitCommitShort is either 7 chars or "unknown"; BuildTimestampUtc, when stamped, is UTC and within the last 365 days and not in the future; all accessors fall back gracefully to "unknown" without throwing or returning null/empty when metadata is missing.
requirements.why: Build metadata is the binary's self-report of what version is deployed; graceful "unknown" fallbacks keep diagnostics working on unstamped local builds.

requirements.statement: The health service aggregates individual check results into an overall status: "healthy" when all checks pass, "unhealthy" when any required check fails, and "degraded" when only optional (non-required) checks fail.
requirements.why: Distinguishing degraded (optional check failed) from unhealthy (required check failed) lets orchestrators keep serving when only non-critical components are down.

requirements.statement: Each health check component reports the correct name, required-ness, and status: the database check (required) is healthy when it can connect and unhealthy on connection failure; the migrations check (required, exposing a "pendingMigrations" count) is unhealthy when migrations are pending; the config check (required) is unhealthy when a required key such as "Hmac:SecretKey" is missing and healthy when all required keys are present; the auth-handlers check (required) is unhealthy when the ApiKey scheme is not registered; the mcp check (optional) is unhealthy when the MCP endpoint is not registered; the temp-writable check (optional) is healthy when it can write and delete a temp file, leaving no temp file behind; the assembly-metadata check (optional) is unhealthy when the git commit is "unknown".
requirements.why: Classifying each check's required-ness correctly is what makes the aggregate healthy/degraded/unhealthy verdict trustworthy for routing decisions.

requirements.statement: The health service bounds every check run (readiness and full) with a 5-second timeout enforced via a cancellation token linked to the caller's token, so an individual check that hangs is cancelled rather than blocking the response indefinitely.
requirements.why: A per-run timeout prevents a single hanging check from stalling the readiness response and tripping the platform's own probe timeout.

requirements.statement: The asset fingerprint manifest omits (rather than errors on) any tracked asset whose physical file is missing, logging a warning and continuing, so a missing asset never fails the /api/v1/health/assets response.
requirements.why: The assets endpoint exists to detect stale bundles; a single missing file must not break that diagnostic by failing the whole response.

requirements.statement: The public "/health" page renders even when running the full health check throws: the exception is swallowed, the health result is treated as null, and the page still returns successfully with no-cache headers.
requirements.why: The /health page must stay reachable precisely when things are broken, so a failing health check cannot be allowed to crash the page itself.

requirements.statement: TotalActive counts the user's tasks whose status is neither Completed nor Cancelled.
requirements.why: TotalActive is the headline "how much is on my plate" number; excluding Completed and Cancelled keeps it to work that still needs doing.

requirements.statement: CompletedToday counts the user's tasks whose completed date falls within the current day.
requirements.why: A "completed today" count gives the user a daily sense of progress and momentum.

requirements.statement: Overdue counts the user's tasks with a target date earlier than today that are not completed; completed tasks past their target date are excluded.
requirements.why: Overdue highlights work that slipped past its target date so the user can triage it; completed-but-late tasks aren't actionable and are excluded.

requirements.statement: InProgress counts only the user's tasks with status InProgress, and Blocked counts only the user's tasks with status Blocked.
requirements.why: Separate InProgress and Blocked counts let the user see active work versus work that is stuck and needs unblocking.

requirements.statement: IncompleteByStatus breaks down the user's active (incomplete) tasks into NotStarted, InProgress, and Blocked counts plus a Total; Completed and Cancelled tasks are excluded, and the Total equals TotalActive.
requirements.why: The Incomplete-by-Status card needs each open-status count plus a Total that reconciles with TotalActive so the user trusts the breakdown.

requirements.statement: ByType groups the user's incomplete tasks by task-type name and reports a count per type (completed tasks excluded).
requirements.why: The breakdown-by-type donut shows the user what kinds of open work dominate their plate; completed tasks would distort the current mix.

requirements.statement: ByPriority groups the user's tasks by priority and reports per-priority breakdown of NotStarted and InProgress counts.
requirements.why: The priority breakdown shows where high-priority work is piling up versus already moving, guiding what to tackle next.

requirements.statement: CompletedPerWeek summarizes the user's completed tasks over the last 12 weeks into per-week counts, with a completion within the current week counted in its week's bucket.
requirements.why: The completed-per-week bar chart shows recent throughput so the user can see their pace trend at a glance.

requirements.statement: CompletionsByArea counts the user's completed tasks separately per area (Personal and Work); non-completed tasks are excluded.
requirements.why: Splitting completions into Personal vs Work shows the user how their finished effort divides across life areas.

requirements.statement: TopTags returns at most the five most-used tags for the user, ordered by descending task count, excluding tags below the cutoff when more than five tags exist.
requirements.why: Capping the tag chart at the top five keeps it readable and surfaces only the user's dominant categories.

requirements.statement: All task statistics are scoped to the requesting user, and an empty database yields zero counts for every metric.
requirements.why: Per-user scoping prevents one user's stats from leaking another's data, and zeroed metrics on an empty DB give new users a clean, non-erroring dashboard.

requirements.statement: CompletedPerMonth summarizes the user's tasks completed within the last 12 months into per-(year, month) counts labelled "YYYY-MM" and ordered ascending by that label.
requirements.why: A 12-month per-month view lets the user see longer-term completion trends and seasonality beyond the weekly chart.

requirements.statement: CompletedPerYear summarizes all of the user's completed tasks (no time cutoff) into per-year counts ordered ascending by year.
requirements.why: An all-time per-year view gives the user a long-horizon record of output across the life of their account.

requirements.statement: CompletionRate pairs, per week over the last 12 weeks, the count of tasks created in that week against the count of tasks completed in that week (keyed by year and week index), with completed defaulting to zero when no completions match a created-week bucket.
requirements.why: Pairing created vs completed per week shows whether the user is keeping up with incoming work or falling behind.

requirements.statement: AvgCompletion reports, per week over the last 12 weeks, the average time-to-complete in days, computed as the mean of (CompletedDate − CreatedDate).TotalDays across that week's completed tasks.
requirements.why: Average time-to-complete per week shows the user whether tasks are turning around faster or lingering longer over time.

requirements.statement: The NotStarted count within IncompleteByStatus is derived arithmetically as TotalActive minus InProgress minus Blocked (avoiding an extra query) and is clamped to a minimum of zero so it can never be negative.
requirements.why: Deriving NotStarted arithmetically avoids an extra DB query, and clamping at zero guards against a nonsensical negative count from any timing skew.

requirements.statement: ByType labels tasks whose task-type association is absent as "Unknown" so every incomplete task contributes to exactly one type bucket.
requirements.why: Bucketing untyped tasks as "Unknown" ensures the by-type totals add up to all incomplete tasks, so the chart never silently drops work.

requirements.statement: TopTags counts only tags attached to the user's non-deleted tasks, so tags on soft-deleted tasks do not contribute to the top-tags ranking.
requirements.why: Excluding soft-deleted tasks keeps the top-tags ranking reflective of live work rather than tags inflated by deleted tasks.

requirements.statement: A tag name must be unique per user: creating or renaming a tag to a name already held by another of the same user's tags is rejected (HTTP 409 / InvalidOperationException). Uniqueness is scoped to the owning user, so two different users may each hold a tag with the same name.
requirements.why: Duplicate tag names within one user would make labels ambiguous in pickers and filters; scoping uniqueness per user avoids forcing a global namespace that would collide across unrelated accounts.

requirements.statement: The per-user duplicate-name check is skipped when a tag update does not change the tag's name (e.g. a color-only edit), so re-saving a tag with its existing name does not raise a conflict.
requirements.why: Skipping the uniqueness check when the name is unchanged lets a color-only edit succeed, since a tag would otherwise always collide with its own existing name.

requirements.statement: Each tag returned in the tag list carries a task count equal to the number of (non-deleted) tasks the tag is assigned to.
requirements.why: SUGGESTED: A per-tag task count lets the user gauge how heavily each label is used and identify unused tags worth pruning; excluding deleted tasks keeps the count truthful.

requirements.statement: A tag create/update request with an invalid payload — an empty name or a color that is not a valid hex color — is rejected as a bad request (HTTP 400).
requirements.why: Rejecting empty names and non-hex colors at the boundary keeps unrenderable or unlabeled tags out of the store, so the UI can always display a valid pill.

requirements.statement: A tag name must not exceed 50 characters; a create or update request whose name is longer is rejected as a bad request (HTTP 400). The 50-character limit is enforced both by request validation and by the persisted column definition.
requirements.why: SUGGESTED: A 50-character cap keeps tag pills compact in the UI and bounds the stored column; enforcing it in both validation and the schema prevents over-long names from slipping in through either path.

requirements.statement: A newly created task receives a sort order of one greater than the user's current maximum task sort order.
requirements.why: Appending new tasks at the end of the user's ordering keeps manual sort positions stable so existing tasks don't shift when one is added.

requirements.statement: When a task is created with status Completed its completion timestamp is set; when created with any non-completed status the completion timestamp is null.
requirements.why: Completion time must be captured the moment a task reaches Completed so completion history and analytics are accurate; non-completed tasks must not carry a false completion time.

requirements.statement: Creating a task writes a single activity-log entry whose field is "Created" and whose new value is the task title.
requirements.why: A create entry gives the activity log a defined starting point so the task's full change history is auditable from inception.

requirements.statement: Deleting a task writes a single activity-log entry whose field is "Deleted" and whose old value is the task title.
requirements.why: Recording deletions in the activity log preserves an audit trail given tasks are soft-deleted rather than hard-deleted.

requirements.statement: Completing a task writes a "Status" activity-log entry recording the task's prior status as the old value and "Completed" as the new value.
requirements.why: Logging the status transition on completion lets users and auditors see when and from what state a task was completed.

requirements.statement: A partial update writes one activity-log entry per field that actually changes, recording the field's old and new values; fields whose value is unchanged produce no activity-log entry.
requirements.why: Logging only fields that actually changed keeps the activity log meaningful and avoids noise from no-op updates.

requirements.statement: A full update writes an activity-log entry for each field whose value differs from the prior stored value.
requirements.why: SUGGESTED: A full update should record every genuine field change so the activity log stays a complete, trustworthy history.

requirements.statement: The incomplete-only filter returns exactly the tasks with status NotStarted, InProgress, or Blocked, excluding Completed and Cancelled tasks.
requirements.why: The incomplete filter exists so users can focus on actionable work, excluding finished or abandoned tasks.

requirements.statement: The overdue-only filter returns exactly the tasks that have a non-null target date in the past and an incomplete status, excluding Completed and Cancelled tasks.
requirements.why: Surfacing overdue work helps users catch commitments they have missed; cancelled and completed tasks are not actionable so are excluded.

requirements.statement: The incomplete-only and overdue-only filters compose conjunctively, returning only tasks that are both incomplete and overdue.
requirements.why: Composing filters conjunctively lets users narrow to exactly the slice they care about (for example work that is both unfinished and late).

requirements.statement: When no incomplete-only or overdue-only filter is supplied, the task listing applies neither filter and returns tasks of all statuses.
requirements.why: Defaulting to no status filter avoids hiding tasks the user did not explicitly choose to hide.

requirements.statement: The default sort order for the task listing is priority descending, then target date ascending with null target dates ordered last.
requirements.why: Priority-then-due default ordering surfaces the most important and most time-sensitive work first; nulls-last keeps undated tasks from crowding the top.

requirements.statement: The task listing can be sorted by title, status, area, or task-type name in either ascending or descending direction; status and area sort by their underlying enum order and type sorts by task-type name.
requirements.why: Letting users sort by any key column makes large task lists navigable to the user's current need.

requirements.statement: When sorting by target date, tasks with no target date always sort last regardless of the sort direction.
requirements.why: Keeping undated tasks last under any direction prevents missing dates from masquerading as earliest or latest, which would mislead the user.

requirements.statement: A cloned task copies the source's description, task type, area, priority, target-date type, and recurrence settings verbatim while receiving a new distinct id.
requirements.why: A clone should reproduce the source's defining attributes so it is a faithful starting copy, while a new id keeps it independent.

requirements.statement: A cloned task is always created with status NotStarted and with a null completion timestamp and null result analysis, regardless of the source task's status.
requirements.why: A clone represents fresh work, so it must start un-started with no carried-over completion state or stale analysis.

requirements.statement: When no title override is supplied (including null, empty, or whitespace-only values), a cloned task's title is the source title with " (copy)" appended.
requirements.why: The copy suffix gives a clone a clearly distinguishable default name so users do not confuse it with the original.

requirements.statement: When a non-blank title override is supplied, the cloned task uses that title.
requirements.why: Honoring an explicit title override lets users name a clone meaningfully at creation time.

requirements.statement: A cloned task's title is truncated so it never exceeds 200 characters, whether the length comes from the copy-suffix derivation or an over-long title override.
requirements.why: Enforcing the 200-char limit on clones keeps clone titles within the same storage and display constraints as any other task.

requirements.statement: A cloned task copies the source target date verbatim when no override is given; a supplied target-date override replaces it; and a clear-target-date flag forces the clone's target date to null, taking precedence over any supplied override.
requirements.why: Clone target-date override semantics let users either reuse, change, or clear the due date so the copy fits its new purpose.

requirements.statement: A cloned task copies all of the source task's tags; if the source has no tags the clone has none.
requirements.why: Copying the source's tags preserves categorization so a clone is filed the same way as its original by default.

requirements.statement: A cloned task receives a sort order of one greater than the user's current maximum task sort order (one when no other tasks exist).
requirements.why: A clone is appended at the end of the ordering for the same reason as any new task: to avoid disturbing existing manual positions.

requirements.statement: Cloning writes exactly one activity-log entry on the new task with field "Created", a null old value, and a new value of "Cloned from {sourceId}".
requirements.why: Recording the clone's origin in its activity log preserves provenance so users can trace where a copied task came from.

requirements.statement: Cloning leaves the source task unchanged: its status, last-modified timestamp, and activity log are not altered.
requirements.why: Cloning must be non-destructive to the source so users can copy freely without side effects on the original.

requirements.statement: Cloning a non-existent, soft-deleted, or another user's task yields no clone (returning not-found at the API), and missing and soft-deleted sources produce the same not-found response.
requirements.why: Returning not-found for inaccessible sources enforces ownership isolation and avoids leaking the existence of other users' or deleted tasks.

requirements.statement: A clone request is valid when its title is absent, null, whitespace-only, or up to 200 characters, and is invalid (rejected) when the supplied title exceeds 200 characters.
requirements.why: Validating the clone title up front prevents invalid clones and gives the user immediate feedback, mirroring create and update rules.

requirements.statement: A clone request's target-date and clear-target-date options are accepted in any combination (clear true, clear false, target date with clear true or false).
requirements.why: Accepting all target-date option combinations keeps the clone API flexible for any due-date intent without surprising rejections.

requirements.statement: A full or partial update never overwrites a field with a null/omitted input value; the existing stored value is retained.
requirements.why: Never overwriting with null protects existing data from being wiped by partial inputs that simply omit a field.

requirements.statement: When a recurring task is completed, the successor task's target date is computed from the source task's target date by adding one day for a Daily pattern, seven days for a Weekly pattern, and one calendar month for a Monthly pattern; if the source has no target date the successor's target date is null.
requirements.why: Computing the successor's due date from the recurrence pattern keeps recurring tasks on their intended cadence automatically.

requirements.statement: A recurring task's successor is created with status NotStarted and copies the source task's title, description, type, area, priority, target-date type, recurrence settings, and all tags.
requirements.why: Carrying the source's attributes into the successor means a recurring task continues unchanged each cycle without manual re-entry.

requirements.statement: A recurring task's successor receives a sort order of one greater than the user's current maximum task sort order.
requirements.why: The successor is appended at the end of the ordering, consistent with all other newly created tasks.

requirements.statement: A successor task is created only when the completed task is both flagged recurring and has a non-null recurrence pattern; completing a task that is recurring but has no recurrence pattern creates no successor.
requirements.why: Requiring both the recurring flag and a pattern prevents creating successors for tasks that were never meant to recur.

requirements.statement: Free-text search of the task list matches case-insensitively against both the task title and the task description.
requirements.why: Searching title and description case-insensitively lets users find tasks by any remembered wording regardless of case.

requirements.statement: The user's maximum task sort order is treated as zero when the user has no tasks, so the first task created for a user receives sort order one.
requirements.why: Treating an empty user as max-order zero makes the first task's sort order deterministic (one) rather than undefined.

requirements.statement: Completing a task sets its completion timestamp to the current time unconditionally, even if a completion timestamp was already present, whereas changing a task to Completed via a full or partial update sets the completion timestamp only when it is currently null (an already-set completion timestamp is preserved).
requirements.why: Distinguishing explicit completion from an update-driven status change preserves an existing completion timestamp during edits while still stamping a true completion event.

requirements.statement: A full update replaces the task's entire tag set with the supplied tag ids (an empty or omitted list clears all tags), whereas a partial update modifies the tag set only when a tag-id list is supplied: a supplied empty list clears all tags, and an omitted (null) list leaves the existing tags unchanged.
requirements.why: Differentiating full-replace from partial tag semantics lets a patch leave tags untouched while a full update authoritatively sets them, matching user expectations of each operation.

requirements.statement: When attaching tags on create, update, or patch, only tag ids that resolve to tags owned by the requesting user are associated; supplied tag ids that do not belong to the user are silently ignored rather than rejected.
requirements.why: Silently ignoring foreign tag ids enforces tag ownership without failing the whole request over a stray id.

requirements.statement: The total page count returned with a paginated task listing is the total matching task count divided by the requested page size, rounded up to the next whole number.
requirements.why: Returning a correct rounded-up page count lets the UI render accurate pagination controls.

requirements.statement: Every explicit column-header sort of the task listing (title, area, type, status, target date, created date, last-modified date, priority) appends the task sort order as a final tie-breaker so that pagination order is deterministic when the primary sort key ties.
requirements.why: A stable sort-order tie-breaker makes paginated results deterministic so rows do not shuffle or duplicate across pages when the primary key ties.

requirements.statement: The task list can additionally be sorted by created date or last-modified date in either direction; these sorts likewise tie-break on sort order.
requirements.why: Sorting by created and last-modified dates lets users find recently added or recently touched tasks; the tie-breaker keeps it deterministic.

requirements.statement: The priority-first default sort (priority ascending, then target date ascending nulls-last, then sort order) is applied only when the incomplete-only filter is active and no explicit sort column is requested; otherwise an unrecognized or default sort key falls back to sorting by priority alone (ascending or descending) with a sort-order tie-breaker.
requirements.why: SUGGESTED: The conditional default sort applies the priority-first ordering only for the focused incomplete view, with a predictable fallback elsewhere to avoid surprising orderings.

requirements.statement: The task list can be filtered to recurring or non-recurring tasks via the is-recurring filter, returning only tasks whose recurring flag matches the supplied value.
requirements.why: The recurring filter lets users isolate or exclude recurring tasks when managing routines versus one-off work.

requirements.statement: When multiple tag ids are supplied as a list filter, the task list returns only tasks that carry every one of the supplied tags (conjunctive tag matching).
requirements.why: Conjunctive tag filtering lets users narrow to tasks carrying every selected tag, matching the AND semantics of the tag picker.

requirements.statement: A task response exposes a human-readable area name derived from the area value: "Work" for Work and "Personal" for any other area value.
requirements.why: Exposing a human-readable area name lets clients display the area without re-implementing the enum-to-label mapping.

requirements.statement: The task types returned exclude inactive types and are ordered ascending by their SortOrder; when no active types exist the result is an empty list.
requirements.why: Hiding inactive types keeps retired options out of selection dropdowns, while SortOrder gives the product control over presentation order independent of id or name.

requirements.statement: An inactive task type is hidden from selection dropdowns but is retained for any existing tasks that already reference it: a task type cannot be deleted while tasks reference it (the task-to-task-type relationship is restricted on delete), so historical tasks keep a valid type even after that type is deactivated.
requirements.why: Deactivating rather than deleting a type, plus a restrict-on-delete relationship, preserves referential integrity so historical tasks keep a valid type instead of pointing at a removed record.

requirements.statement: GET /api/v1/activity-logs returns the user's task change-history entries as a paginated list honoring page and pageSize parameters, returning an empty list with zero total count for a user with no activity.
requirements.why: Scoping change history to the requesting user and paginating it prevents cross-user leakage and keeps long histories navigable.

requirements.statement: GET /api/v1/activity-logs accepts a taskId filter and returns only the change-history entries belonging to that task.
requirements.why: The taskId filter powers the per-task activity log on the task detail view, so it must return only that task's history.

requirements.statement: Creating a task records an activity-log entry with fieldChanged "Created", and updating a task records an activity-log entry for that task.
requirements.why: Every write operation must leave an audit trail, so creates and updates each record a change-history entry.

requirements.statement: Deleting a task records an activity-log entry with fieldChanged "Deleted", and that entry (and the task's prior history) remains visible via the activity-log API even after the task is soft-deleted.
requirements.why: Soft-delete preserves the record, so a deleted task's history must remain auditable rather than vanishing with the task.

requirements.statement: Each activity-log entry exposes id, taskId, taskTitle, timestamp, fieldChanged, oldValue, newValue, and changedBy fields.
requirements.why: SUGGESTED: These fields are what the activity-log view renders per entry — old/new values and who changed them make each change self-describing.

requirements.statement: GET /api/v1/activity-logs accepts optional filters applied conjunctively when present: taskId (exact), from/to (Timestamp >= from and <= to), fieldChanged (exact match), and changedBy (case-sensitive substring match); paging defaults to page 1 with a page size of 50 when unspecified.
requirements.why: Conjunctive filters let an owner narrow change history to a task, time window, field, or actor when reviewing what changed.

requirements.statement: GET /api/v1/activity-logs returns entries ordered by Timestamp descending (most recent first), and each entry's taskTitle is resolved from the owning task's current title at query time (including soft-deleted tasks).
requirements.why: Most-recent-first ordering surfaces the latest changes first, and resolving taskTitle at query time (even for soft-deleted tasks) keeps each entry readable rather than showing a bare ID.

requirements.statement: Creating an API key (POST /api/v1/apikeys with a name) returns 201 and exposes the full plain-text key exactly once in the response; the key's prefix equals the first 8 characters of that plain-text key.
requirements.why: Only the hash is stored, so the plain-text key can never be recovered later — it must be shown to the caller exactly once at creation or it is lost.

requirements.statement: GET /api/v1/apikeys returns all of the user's API keys, and key listing responses never expose the plain-text key or the stored key hash.
requirements.why: Exposing the plain-text key or stored hash on a list endpoint would defeat the show-once secret model and leak credentials usable against the REST API.

requirements.statement: POST /api/v1/apikeys/{id}/deactivate marks the key inactive (isActive=false) and POST /api/v1/apikeys/{id}/activate marks it active again (isActive=true), each returning 204.
requirements.why: Lets an owner instantly suspend a key suspected of misuse without permanently revoking it, so legitimate access can be restored later.

requirements.statement: DELETE /api/v1/apikeys/{id} revokes the key (returns 204), after which it no longer appears in the user's key list.
requirements.why: Permanent revocation must remove the key from the owner's management view so a compromised credential cannot be reactivated or mistaken for a live key.

requirements.statement: PATCH /api/v1/apikeys/{id}/rename sets the key's name to the supplied value and returns 204; renaming a non-existent key returns 404.
requirements.why: SUGGESTED: Lets owners relabel a key to track which LLM client uses it without rotating the credential; renaming a missing key must 404 rather than silently no-op.

requirements.statement: GET /api/v1/apikeys returns the user's keys ordered alphabetically by name (ascending), and each listed key exposes id, name, keyPrefix, createdDate, lastUsedDate, and isActive.
requirements.why: SUGGESTED: Alphabetical ordering and a stable field set give the keys-management table a predictable layout for owners scanning many keys.

requirements.statement: Creating an API key requires a non-empty name of at most 100 characters; a missing/blank name or a name exceeding 100 characters is rejected with a validation error (400) and the key is not created.
requirements.why: A required, length-bounded name keeps the key list human-readable and prevents unlabeled or oversized labels from being persisted.

requirements.statement: A successful key validation updates that key's LastUsedDate to the current UTC time, so the lastUsedDate subsequently reflects the most recent successful use of the key.
requirements.why: lastUsedDate lets an owner spot stale or unexpectedly active keys and decide which to revoke.

requirements.statement: The audit page presents two tabs — "Task History" and "API Access" — and opens on the Task History tab by default when no tab is specified.
requirements.why: SUGGESTED: Task History is the more frequently consulted view, so it is the sensible default landing tab on the audit page.

requirements.statement: When the user has no task change history, the Task History tab shows an empty-state message instead of a populated history table.
requirements.why: An explicit empty state reassures the user that there is genuinely no history rather than a load failure or empty table glitch.

requirements.statement: After a task is edited, the Task History tab displays the resulting change-history entries for that user.
requirements.why: The Task History tab exists to let the owner see what changed on a task and when, so edits must surface as visible history entries.

requirements.statement: The API Access tab displays summary cards including "Total Requests" and "Active API Keys".
requirements.why: Summary cards give the owner an at-a-glance read on how much LLM API traffic is hitting their account and how many keys are live.

requirements.statement: When the user has no API access logs, the API Access tab shows an empty-state message instead of a populated log list.
requirements.why: An empty state confirms there has been no API activity rather than leaving the user staring at a blank or seemingly broken log.

requirements.statement: The user can switch from the Task History tab to the API Access tab, which then renders the API access summary content.
GET /api/v1/audit returns the requesting user's API access audit logs as a paginated list, honoring page and pageSize parameters and returning an empty list when the user has no logs.
requirements.why: Scoping audit logs to the requesting user and paginating them prevents cross-tenant data exposure and keeps large log volumes navigable.

requirements.statement: GET /api/v1/audit/summary returns the requesting user's API usage summary comprising totalRequests, getsToday, writesToday, and activeApiKeys, all zero for a user with no API activity.
requirements.why: The summary endpoint backs the dashboard cards, so it must return the same per-user totals and zero them for a user with no activity.

requirements.statement: GET /api/v1/audit returns the user's API access logs ordered by Timestamp descending (most recent first).
requirements.why: Most-recent-first ordering puts the activity an owner most likely wants to review at the top of the audit log.

requirements.statement: GET /api/v1/audit accepts optional filters that are applied conjunctively when present: apiKeyId (exact), from/to (Timestamp >= from and <= to), httpMethod (exact match), statusCodeMin (ResponseStatusCode >= value) and statusCodeMax (ResponseStatusCode <= value); paging defaults to page 1 with a page size of 50 when unspecified.
requirements.why: Conjunctive filters let an owner narrow a large audit log to a specific key, time window, method, or status range when investigating API activity.

requirements.statement: Each audit access-log entry exposes id, apiKeyId, apiKeyName, timestamp, httpMethod, endpoint, requestBodyHash, responseStatusCode, and durationMs.
requirements.why: SUGGESTED: These fields are what the audit table renders per row, and requestBodyHash records what was sent without ever storing the full body.

requirements.statement: The LLM Audit Dashboard (API Access tab) presents a per-API-key bar chart showing request count per API key over the last 30 days.
requirements.why: A per-key bar chart over 30 days lets an owner visually spot which LLM client drives traffic and detect unexpected spikes.

requirements.statement: On the LLM Audit Dashboard (API Access tab), clicking an API key name filters the audit-log table to that key's activity, and the available filters include an API-key dropdown and a status-code range in addition to date range and HTTP method.
requirements.why: Click-to-filter and an API-key dropdown plus status-code range let an owner drill straight into one key's activity or isolate error responses without hand-editing filters.

requirements.statement: A new user can register with an email and password, which creates an account and returns the new user's id; on the web UI a successful registration signs the user in and redirects them to the dashboard.
requirements.why: Registration is the entry point for the owner to obtain an account; auto sign-in plus dashboard redirect removes a friction step so a new user lands in a usable state immediately.

requirements.statement: Registering with an email that is already in use is rejected as a bad request (HTTP 400) and no duplicate account is created.
requirements.why: Email is the unique account identifier; allowing a duplicate would create ambiguous accounts and let one registration silently shadow or hijack another.

requirements.statement: A user who logs in with valid credentials is authenticated (an auth cookie is set), the response returns their user details, and on the web UI they are redirected away from the login page to the dashboard.
requirements.why: Cookie-based login is the gate for all owner web access; setting the auth cookie and redirecting off the login page is what establishes and confirms the authenticated session.

requirements.statement: A login attempt with an incorrect password is rejected (HTTP 401) and is not authenticated; on the web UI the user remains on the login page and is shown an invalid-credentials error message.
requirements.why: Rejecting bad credentials without authenticating is the core protection against unauthorized access; the 401 and on-page error give the user clear feedback without leaking which factor was wrong.

requirements.statement: An authenticated user can log out, which clears their session (HTTP 204 on the API); on the web UI logging out redirects the user to the login page.
requirements.why: Logout must reliably terminate the session so a shared or unattended device cannot retain owner access after the user intends to leave.

requirements.statement: An authenticated user can retrieve their own current account details (id and email) via the "me" endpoint.
requirements.why: A "me" endpoint lets the UI and API clients confirm who the current session belongs to without exposing other users' data.

requirements.statement: An authenticated user can change their own password by supplying their current password and a new password; on success the change is applied and HTTP 204 (No Content) is returned, while a failed change (e.g. wrong current password or a new password that violates password policy) is rejected as a bad request (HTTP 400) with per-error field details.
requirements.why: Requiring the current password before a change prevents a hijacked session from silently locking out the real owner; per-field errors guide the user to a compliant new password.

requirements.statement: On a successful web-UI login, the user is redirected to the supplied returnUrl when one is present, falling back to the site root ("/") otherwise; the redirect is performed as a local redirect, so an off-site returnUrl is not honored.
requirements.why: Honoring returnUrl restores the user's intended destination after login, while restricting it to local redirects blocks open-redirect attacks that could send the user to a malicious off-site URL.

requirements.statement: Web-UI logout is performed only via POST; issuing a GET to the logout page does not sign the user out and instead redirects to the site root ("/").
requirements.why: Restricting logout to POST prevents CSRF-style forced logout via a planted GET link or prefetched image, so a third party cannot sign the owner out unexpectedly.

requirements.statement: The application exposes a "/changelog" page that, for an authenticated user, renders the version history including a "What's new" heading and per-version entries showing rendered version numbers (e.g. "v1.2"), never raw/unevaluated template expressions.
requirements.why: Users learn what shipped from /changelog; unrendered template expressions would expose a broken release-notes surface.

requirements.statement: The sidebar contains a changelog navigation link (the "What's new" affordance) that navigates to the "/changelog" page when clicked.
requirements.why: The "What's new" affordance is how users discover the release-notes page; without a working link the page is unreachable.

requirements.statement: Each changelog version entry displays a version-type badge (including a "Major" badge for major releases) and one or more change-type badges drawn from the set Feature / Fix / Improvement.
requirements.why: Type badges let users scan at a glance which releases are major and what kind of changes each entry contains.

requirements.statement: The dashboard (home) page displays five summary cards: Total Active, Completed Today, Overdue, In Progress, and Blocked.
requirements.why: The summary cards give the user an at-a-glance read on their workload (active, due, overdue, blocked) the moment they land on the home page.

requirements.statement: The dashboard renders a charts section containing visualizations such as "Completed per Week" and "By Priority".
requirements.why: The charts turn raw task history into trends (throughput, priority mix) so the user can see productivity patterns over time.

requirements.statement: The dashboard provides a quick-add form that creates a new task from a title and returns to the dashboard.
requirements.why: Quick-add lets the user capture a task in one field without leaving the dashboard, removing friction from the most common action.

requirements.statement: Dashboard summary cards and the incomplete-status sub-tiles link to the filtered Tasks view: the not-started tile navigates to the tasks list filtered by status=NotStarted (with active tasks as the default scope), and the overdue card navigates to the tasks list filtered by overdue=true (with active tasks as the default scope).
requirements.why: Making cards and tiles click-through to the matching filtered list turns each metric into a direct path to act on it.

requirements.statement: The dashboard provides navigation links to the Tasks page (/tasks) and the Audit page (/audit).
requirements.why: SUGGESTED: The dashboard is the landing page, so it must offer direct routes to the primary work areas (Tasks and Audit).

requirements.statement: Dashboard quick-add ignores a null or whitespace-only title (redirecting without creating a task); a valid title is trimmed and creates a task with fixed defaults — task type 1 (Task), area Personal, priority Medium, status NotStarted, target-date-type ThisWeek, not recurring — and surfaces a "created" toast.
requirements.why: Sensible fixed defaults let one-field quick-add produce a valid task instantly, while ignoring blank titles prevents accidental empty tasks.

requirements.statement: The dashboard "recent tasks" list shows the user's 10 most recently modified tasks, requested with page size 10 sorted by last-modified date descending.
requirements.why: SUGGESTED: Showing the 10 most recently touched tasks gives the user a fast way back to what they were just working on.

requirements.statement: GET /api/v1/health/version returns 200 with a payload exposing the build version, full git commit, and short git commit, matching the values stamped into the assembly; the response carries no-cache headers (Cache-Control no-store, Pragma no-cache, Expires 0) and custom X-TaskPilot-Version and X-TaskPilot-Commit headers.
requirements.why: Post-deploy verification needs an unambiguous, uncacheable way to confirm exactly which build and commit is live on an instance.

requirements.statement: GET /api/v1/health/live always returns 200 with status "alive".
requirements.why: A dependency-free liveness probe lets orchestrators (Azure Always On, uptime monitors) confirm the process is up without coupling to DB health.

requirements.statement: GET /api/v1/health/ready returns 200 with status "healthy" or "degraded" when all required checks pass, and 503 with status "unhealthy" when a required check (e.g. database) is unhealthy.
requirements.why: Readiness must return 503 when a required dependency is down so the platform stops routing traffic to an instance that cannot serve requests.

requirements.statement: GET /api/v1/health/full returns the aggregate status plus a per-check array including the checks database, migrations, config, auth-handlers, mcp, temp-writable, and assembly-metadata, where each check carries a non-null duration; it returns 200 (status "healthy" or "degraded") when only optional checks fail and 503 (status "unhealthy") when a required check such as migrations fails.
requirements.why: The deep per-check breakdown lets an operator diagnose which component degraded an instance without shelling into the host.

requirements.statement: GET /api/v1/health/assets returns 200 with an asset manifest mapping each asset path to its SHA-256 integrity hash (prefixed "sha256-"); the hashes are stable across repeated calls and match the SHA-256 of the actually served asset bytes.
requirements.why: A SHA-256 asset manifest lets operators detect a stale or CDN-cached bundle that no longer matches the deployed build.

requirements.statement: All /api/v1/health/* endpoints (live, ready, full, version, assets) are accessible anonymously (never returning 401 or 403).
requirements.why: Health endpoints must stay anonymous so external probes and uptime monitors can reach them without credentials.

requirements.statement: The application exposes a public "/health" page (loadable anonymously, never redirecting to login) that renders the overall health status badge, the build version, and the short git commit consistent with the /api/v1/health endpoints, lists at least seven per-check rows each showing name/status/duration, and provides a "raw JSON" link that navigates to /api/v1/health/full.
requirements.why: A human-readable /health page lets anyone inspect a deployed instance's status and version at a glance without calling the API directly.

requirements.statement: The sidebar shows a version pill displaying the current build version and short git commit (matching /api/v1/health/version) that links to the "/health" page.
requirements.why: The version pill gives every user an always-visible, authoritative indicator of the running build that links straight to diagnostics.

requirements.statement: The /api/v1/health/version and /api/v1/health/full|ready responses expose an uptime computed as the difference between current UTC time and the process start time, plus the runtime environment name and machine name.
requirements.why: Uptime, environment, and machine name help operators spot recent restarts and confirm they are inspecting the intended instance.

requirements.statement: The application exposes an "/integrations" page that loads for an authenticated user without an unhandled error or 404, and the sidebar contains a navigation link to it.
requirements.why: The Integrations page is how users learn to connect LLMs/automation to the API, so it must be reachable from the sidebar and load cleanly.

requirements.statement: The Integrations page documents how to use the API: an API-key / quick-start section, a curl example, a Claude tool definition, an OpenAI function definition, an "MCP coming soon" section, and a reference to the Swagger/API docs.
requirements.why: Copy-ready quick-start, curl, and per-provider tool definitions give users everything needed to wire an LLM to TaskPilot without leaving the app.

requirements.statement: Code/snippet blocks on the Integrations page provide a copy button that, when clicked, gives copied feedback without producing an unhandled error.
requirements.why: One-click copy of long tool definitions and curl commands avoids error-prone manual selection of multi-line snippets.

requirements.statement: The Settings page surfaces an API Reference section that links to or references the Integrations documentation.
requirements.why: SUGGESTED: Users who just created an API key on Settings need a discoverable path to the integration docs that show how to use it.

requirements.statement: The Tasks page "show" scope accepts "active", "completed", or "all"; an omitted or unrecognized value falls back to "active" (NotStarted, InProgress, Blocked), and the "view" parameter falls back to "list" for anything other than "board".
requirements.why: Defaulting an omitted or garbage scope/view to safe values ("active"/"list") means a hand-edited or stale URL still renders a sensible Tasks page.

requirements.statement: For the "active" show scope the Tasks page requests only incomplete tasks from the repository; for the "completed" scope it fetches all tasks and then post-filters at the page layer to only Completed and Cancelled tasks; "all" returns every status.
requirements.why: SUGGESTED: Querying only incomplete tasks for the default "active" scope keeps the common view fast, while broader scopes fetch more and filter in the page layer.

requirements.statement: When no sort column is supplied in the URL, the Tasks page leaves SortBy/SortDir null for header-state purposes but passes the repository default sort of "priority" ascending; an explicit sortDir is normalized to "desc" only when equal to "desc" (case-insensitive), otherwise "asc", and sortBy is lower-cased.
requirements.why: Normalizing sort inputs (and defaulting to priority asc) gives a predictable, abuse-tolerant ordering while keeping header chevron state accurate to the URL.

requirements.statement: The Tasks board (kanban) view renders three columns (Not Started, In Progress, Blocked) for the "active" scope, two columns (Completed, Cancelled) for "completed", and all five columns for "all", each populated by filtering the fetched tasks by status.
requirements.why: Showing only the columns relevant to the current scope keeps the kanban focused (open work vs done) instead of cluttering it with empty states.

requirements.statement: The Tasks page treats filters as active (driving the "Reset filters" affordance) when the show scope is not "active", or any of status / priority / area / task-type / tag / overdue filters is set, or an explicit sort column is present.
requirements.why: Knowing when any filter/sort deviates from the default lets the page show a "Reset filters" affordance so users can escape a narrowed view in one click.

requirements.statement: The Tasks page reports TotalCount as the number of tasks shown after the page-layer post-filter for the current scope (i.e. the size of the rendered list), not the repository's unpaged total.
requirements.why: Reporting the post-filter count means the displayed total matches what the user actually sees, not a larger pre-filter number that would look wrong.

requirements.statement: Creating a task from the Tasks page rejects a whitespace-only title with an error toast and no creation; on success the new task is created with IsRecurring false and a success toast is shown via post-redirect-get.
requirements.why: Rejecting blank titles prevents empty tasks, and post-redirect-get with a toast confirms success while avoiding duplicate creates on refresh.

requirements.statement: The application supports global keyboard shortcuts as specified in REQUIREMENTS.md §4.8: N (new task), E (edit selected task), / (focus search), Esc (close slide-over/modal), ? (show keyboard-shortcuts overlay), and Space (toggle selected task complete); the quick-add bar also supports title+Tab to open the full create form pre-filled.
requirements.why: Global keyboard shortcuts let power users drive the app (create, edit, complete, search) without reaching for the mouse, speeding repetitive task management.

requirements.statement: The MCP "list tasks" tool returns the user's tasks as a serialized paged result; an optional status filter string is parsed into the corresponding task-status enum and applied to the query, and an unrecognized status string raises an argument error.
requirements.why: list_tasks is the LLM's primary read path; rejecting an unrecognized status string surfaces a clear error instead of silently returning wrong results.

requirements.statement: The MCP "get task" tool returns the requested task serialized when it exists, and raises an invalid-operation error when no task matches the id.
requirements.why: An explicit error for an unknown id lets the calling LLM distinguish "no such task" from a transient failure and recover.

requirements.statement: The MCP "create task" tool creates a task for the calling user from the supplied fields and returns the serialized task.
requirements.why: create_task is the core write capability that lets an LLM add work on the user's behalf; returning the serialized task confirms what was created.

requirements.statement: The MCP "update task" tool raises an invalid-operation error when the target task does not exist.
requirements.why: Failing loudly on a missing target prevents an LLM update from silently no-op'ing against a task that doesn't exist or isn't the user's.

requirements.statement: The MCP "complete task" tool marks the task complete (forwarding an optional result-analysis note) and returns the serialized task.
requirements.why: Letting the LLM mark tasks complete with an optional result note captures outcomes at the moment work finishes.

requirements.statement: The MCP "delete task" tool returns a success result when the task is deleted, and raises an invalid-operation error when the task does not exist.
requirements.why: A distinct success vs invalid-operation result lets the LLM confirm a delete happened rather than assuming it did.

requirements.statement: The MCP toolset exposes read tools that return serialized stats, the user's tag list, and the active task-type list.
requirements.why: Exposing stats, tags, and task-types as read tools gives the LLM the context it needs to create and filter tasks with valid values.

requirements.statement: The MCP "clone_task" tool duplicates an existing task for the calling user (defaulting the clone title to "<source title> (copy)" when no title override is given, honouring a target-date override or a clear-target-date flag) and raises an invalid-operation error when the source task does not exist or cannot be cloned.
requirements.why: Clone lets the LLM spin up a near-duplicate task (e.g. a recurring chore) without re-specifying every field, with a sensible "(copy)" title default.

requirements.statement: The MCP "list_tasks" tool caps the effective page size at 100 (clamping any larger requested pageSize down to 100) before querying.
requirements.why: Capping page size at 100 protects the server from an LLM requesting an unbounded page that could exhaust memory or time out.

requirements.statement: MCP enum-valued parameters are parsed case-insensitively; an unrecognized value raises an argument error whose message enumerates the valid values, and for optional filter parameters a null/omitted value is treated as "no filter" while required create parameters reject a null/invalid value.
requirements.why: Case-insensitive parsing plus an error that lists valid values lets an LLM self-correct after passing a wrong enum, raising tool-call success rates.

requirements.statement: The "/settings" page presents an API Keys section, an Appearance section, and a Change Password section (with a current-password input), all rendering without an unhandled error.
requirements.why: Settings is the single place a user manages account access — API keys, appearance, and password — so all three sections must be present and functional.

requirements.statement: On the Settings page a user generates an API key by entering a key name and submitting; the newly created key value (e.g. a "tp_"-prefixed token with a copy affordance) is displayed once on creation.
requirements.why: The raw key is only recoverable at creation since it is stored hashed; showing it once with a copy affordance is the user's sole chance to save it.

requirements.statement: On the Settings page a user can create a tag (name) and then edit it inline to rename and recolor it; the changes persist and are reflected across the page. The inline edit can be completed keyboard-only (focus the edit affordance, press Enter to open, type, press Enter to save).
requirements.why: Inline rename/recolor lets users curate tags in place, and keyboard-only completion keeps the flow accessible without a mouse.

requirements.statement: Renaming a tag to a name that already exists is rejected with an inline "already exists" error, and the edit row remains open with the failing input still visible (no redirect).
requirements.why: Blocking duplicate tag names inline (keeping the row open) prevents ambiguous tags while letting the user fix the name without losing context.

requirements.statement: On the Settings page, generating an API key with a null or whitespace-only name is ignored (redirect without creating a key); a valid name is trimmed before the key is created.
requirements.why: Ignoring blank key names avoids creating unlabelled keys the user can't later tell apart in the keys table.

requirements.statement: When creating or updating a tag with a blank color, the Settings page defaults the color to "#64748B" before validation and persistence.
requirements.why: Defaulting a blank color to a neutral slate guarantees every tag chip renders a visible color dot rather than appearing broken.

requirements.statement: The Settings page only treats the "editTagId" query parameter (or the tag being edited after a validation/conflict error) as the open edit row when that tag actually belongs to the current user's tag set; otherwise no edit row is opened.
requirements.why: Scoping the edit row to the user's own tags stops a guessed or tampered editTagId from opening or exposing another user's tag.

requirements.statement: A failed password change on the Settings page re-renders the page in place (no redirect) with the concatenated identity error descriptions shown and the API-keys and tags lists reloaded; a successful change redirects with a success toast.
requirements.why: Re-rendering in place with the identity errors lets the user see exactly why a password change failed without losing the rest of the page state.

requirements.statement: Updating a tag that resolves to no record (not found for the user) aborts with a "Tag not found" error message via redirect rather than re-rendering the inline edit row.
requirements.why: A tag that no longer exists (or isn't the user's) can't have an edit row, so the flow aborts cleanly with a message instead of rendering a stale form.

requirements.statement: The Settings page provides a Data Export action that exports the user's tasks as a CSV file.
requirements.why: CSV export lets users get their own task data out of the app for backup or analysis, avoiding lock-in.

requirements.statement: A user can create a tag with a name and a color, which persists the tag (HTTP 201) and returns it with the supplied color.
requirements.why: Tags are the user's own organizing labels; persisting the chosen color is what lets tasks render as recognizable colored pills across the UI.

requirements.statement: A user can list all of their own tags.
requirements.why: SUGGESTED: Listing the user's tags is what populates tag pickers and filters; scoping to the owner keeps one user's labels out of another's view.

requirements.statement: A user can update an existing tag's name and color, and the updated values are returned.
requirements.why: Editing name and color lets the user correct or rebrand a label without recreating it and losing its task associations.

requirements.statement: A user can delete one of their own tags (HTTP 204).
requirements.why: Users need to retire labels they no longer use; deletion removes the tag from all tasks so stale labels do not clutter pickers and filters.

requirements.statement: Updating a tag that does not exist returns not-found (HTTP 404).
requirements.why: A 404 distinguishes a missing resource from a malformed request, giving API clients an accurate, actionable signal instead of a false success.

requirements.statement: The user's tags are returned ordered ascending by tag name.
requirements.why: SUGGESTED: Alphabetical ordering gives a stable, predictable list so users can scan and locate a tag quickly in pickers and filters.

requirements.statement: A user can create a task with a title, description, type, area, priority, status, target-date type, optional target date, recurrence settings, and optional tags, and the created task is persisted and returned.
requirements.why: Task creation is the core action of the app; capturing all task fields up front lets users record complete work items.

requirements.statement: A task can be created with one or more tags attached, and those tags are associated with the task and appear in its representation.
requirements.why: Allowing tags at creation lets users categorize a task immediately rather than in a follow-up edit.

requirements.statement: A user can retrieve a single task by its id, receiving its full details, and a request for a non-existent task returns not-found.
requirements.why: Single-task retrieval backs detail views and edit flows; not-found signals a missing or inaccessible task clearly.

requirements.statement: A user can complete a task, which sets its status to Completed, records the completion timestamp, and optionally stores a result-analysis note.
requirements.why: Completing a task with optional result analysis captures both the outcome and the user's reflection for later review.

requirements.statement: Completing a recurring task creates a successor task in addition to completing the current one.
requirements.why: Auto-creating a successor on completing a recurring task removes the manual work of re-entering routine tasks.

requirements.statement: A user can delete a task, after which it no longer appears in listings or single-task retrieval.
requirements.why: Soft-deleting and hiding a task lets users clear their list while preserving an audit trail and an undo window.

requirements.statement: A user can fully update an existing task's editable fields, and the updated values are persisted and returned.
requirements.why: Full update lets users edit any editable field of an existing task and persist the result.

requirements.statement: A user can partially update a task by supplying only selected fields; supplied fields are changed while omitted (null) fields retain their existing values.
requirements.why: Partial update lets clients and the API change selected fields without resending the whole task or risking unintended overwrites.

requirements.statement: A user can list their tasks as a paginated collection.
requirements.why: Paginated listing keeps the task view performant and navigable as the number of tasks grows.

requirements.statement: A user can filter the task list by free-text search, status, area, task type, and tags (with tag filtering requiring all supplied tags to match).
requirements.why: Combinable filters let users quickly find the specific tasks they need among many.

requirements.statement: A user can retrieve task statistics, including total active count and a breakdown of incomplete tasks by status.
requirements.why: Task statistics power the dashboard summary cards that give users an at-a-glance sense of their workload.

requirements.statement: A user can clone an existing task, producing a new independent task whose creation is acknowledged with a location reference to the new task and which is immediately retrievable.
requirements.why: Cloning lets users start a new task from an existing one, saving re-entry for similar work.

requirements.statement: A user can create a task through the Tasks page UI (via the New Task modal), and the new task then appears in the task list.
requirements.why: The New Task modal is the primary UI path for creating tasks for web users.

requirements.statement: A user can create a task through a quick-add input from the dashboard, and the new task then appears in the task list.
requirements.why: Dashboard quick-add lets users capture a task in one step without leaving the dashboard.

requirements.statement: When creating a task in the UI, the Area control defaults to Personal.
requirements.why: Defaulting Area to Personal matches the most common case and reduces required clicks on create.

requirements.statement: A user can create a new tag inline from within the task-create modal, and the new tag immediately appears in the modal's tag list and can be assigned to the task being created.
requirements.why: Inline tag creation lets users categorize a task without breaking flow to a separate tag-management screen.

requirements.statement: A user can open a task's detail page to view and edit its fields, and editing a field then saving records the change in the task's change history.
requirements.why: The detail page is where users review and edit a task; logging edits keeps the change history complete.

requirements.statement: A user can delete a task from its detail page, after which it is removed from the task list.
requirements.why: Deleting from the detail page lets users remove a task while viewing it, without returning to the list first.

requirements.statement: The Tasks page offers both a list view and a board (kanban) view, switchable via a view toggle, with the board view rendering tasks in status columns.
requirements.why: Offering list and board views lets users choose between dense scanning and status-based kanban workflow.

requirements.statement: On the Tasks page the user can filter the list with a search input, which narrows results and shows an empty state when nothing matches.
requirements.why: In-page search lets users narrow a long task list quickly; the empty state confirms a no-match result rather than a broken page.

requirements.statement: An overdue task row displays a textual "Overdue" pill alongside its target date.
requirements.why: An explicit Overdue pill (not color alone) flags late tasks accessibly so users notice missed deadlines.

requirements.statement: The Tasks page provides an Overdue filter chip that toggles its pressed state and adds or removes overdue=true from the page URL.
requirements.why: The Overdue chip lets users toggle a late-work view, and reflecting it in the URL makes the view shareable and bookmarkable.

requirements.statement: Clicking a sortable column header on the Tasks list cycles its sort through ascending, descending, then off, reflecting the state in the URL (sortBy/sortDir) and the header's aria-sort attribute.
requirements.why: Cycling column-header sort with URL and aria-sort state gives users familiar, accessible, shareable sorting.

requirements.statement: Sorting via a column header preserves the other active filters (such as area) in the URL.
requirements.why: Preserving other filters when sorting prevents losing the user's current view context on a header click.

requirements.statement: The Tasks page has an Active/Completed/All segmented control: Active (the default) shows only NotStarted/InProgress/Blocked tasks, Completed shows only Completed/Cancelled tasks, and All shows every status; the selected segment is reflected in the URL and its pressed state.
requirements.why: The Active/Completed/All control lets users focus on current work by default while still reaching finished or all tasks; URL state makes it shareable.

requirements.statement: An unrecognized show value on the Tasks page is treated as the default Active view.
requirements.why: Falling back to the default Active view on a bad show value prevents a broken or empty page from a malformed URL.

requirements.statement: The Tasks page show segment composes with other filters (overdue and priority), returning only tasks matching both the segment and the additional filter.
requirements.why: Composing the show segment with other filters lets users combine status focus with overdue and priority narrowing.

requirements.statement: The board (kanban) view renders columns matching the active show segment: three open-status columns for Active and the two terminal-status columns for Completed.
requirements.why: Matching board columns to the active segment keeps the kanban consistent with the chosen status scope.

requirements.statement: Tasks-page filter selections are persisted per browser session and restored when the user navigates back to the Tasks page (via sidebar or address bar), without producing a navigation/redirect loop; a fresh session starts at the default Active view.
requirements.why: Persisting filters per session restores the user's working view on return without redirect loops, improving continuity.

requirements.statement: A Reset Filters action on the Tasks page clears the persisted filter state and returns the page to the default Active view.
requirements.why: A Reset Filters action gives users a one-click escape back to the default view when filters get confusing.

requirements.statement: After login the dashboard shows summary cards including Total Active and Overdue counts.
requirements.why: Dashboard summary cards give users an immediate sense of active and overdue workload after login.

requirements.statement: Creating or fully updating a task is rejected when the title is empty, when the title exceeds 200 characters, or when the task type id is not greater than zero.
requirements.why: Title and task-type validation prevents creating malformed or unidentifiable tasks.

requirements.statement: Creating or fully updating a task is rejected when the target-date type is SpecificDay but no target date is supplied.
requirements.why: Requiring a date for SpecificDay prevents an inconsistent task that claims a specific day with no date.

requirements.statement: Creating or fully updating a task is rejected when the task is flagged recurring but no recurrence pattern is supplied, or when the supplied recurrence pattern is not a defined pattern value.
requirements.why: Requiring a valid recurrence pattern when recurring prevents recurring tasks that cannot compute a successor.

requirements.statement: Creating or fully updating a task is rejected when the priority, status, area, or target-date-type value is not a defined enum value.
requirements.why: Rejecting out-of-range enum values prevents corrupt enum state that downstream logic and storage cannot interpret.

requirements.statement: A user can reorder a task by setting its sort order to an explicit value; the operation succeeds only for a task owned by the user and otherwise reports failure.
requirements.why: Explicit reorder lets the ordering be set programmatically while ownership checks prevent reordering another user's tasks.

requirements.statement: The application provides global keyboard shortcuts for task workflows: `N` opens the new-task create panel, `E` edits the selected task, `/` focuses the search input, `Esc` closes the active slide-over or modal, `?` shows a keyboard-shortcuts overlay, and `Space` toggles the selected task complete.
requirements.why: SUGGESTED: Keyboard shortcuts speed up power-user task workflows without reaching for the mouse.

requirements.statement: The task create/edit slide-over offers a "Save & Create Another" action that saves the current task and immediately reopens an empty create form for rapid batch entry.
requirements.why: SUGGESTED: Save and Create Another speeds up entering many tasks in one sitting.

requirements.statement: The task create/edit form auto-saves an in-progress draft to `localStorage` if the user navigates away mid-edit, so the unsaved input can be restored.
requirements.why: SUGGESTED: Auto-saving a draft protects users from losing in-progress input if they navigate away mid-edit.

requirements.statement: A task's Description supports markdown rendering in the UI (the stored text is rendered as formatted markdown when displayed).
requirements.why: SUGGESTED: Markdown rendering lets users format task descriptions for readability.

requirements.statement: A user can reorder tasks within a view by drag-and-drop, persisting the new manual `SortOrder`. (Distinct from FR-TASKS-036, which covers the service-level `UpdateSortOrderAsync` method: this record covers the user-facing drag-and-drop interaction and the HTTP/UI surface that drives it.)
requirements.why: SUGGESTED: Drag-and-drop reordering gives users an intuitive way to set manual task priority order.

requirements.statement: On mobile, swipe gestures on a task row perform quick actions: swipe right marks the task complete, and swipe left soft-deletes it with an undo toast.
